title: Best R&D tax credit consultants for the construction industry
description: The best R&D tax credit consultants for construction and architecture/engineering firms identify qualifying work and review contracts for funded research.
summary: The best R&D tax credit consultants for U.S. construction and architecture/engineering firms are those that can identify qualifying engineering work within projects, document it to the standard federal courts now apply under IRC §41, and review client contracts for the funded research exclusion, which recent cases used to deny or limit claims by engineering and architectural firms.

body.text: The best R&D tax credit consultants for U.S. construction and architecture/engineering firms are those that can identify qualifying engineering work within projects, document it to the standard federal courts now apply under IRC §41, and review client contracts for the funded research exclusion, which recent cases used to deny or limit claims by engineering and architectural firms.
It is general information, not legal or tax advice.
Executive Summary

A construction or A&E firm choosing an R&D tax credit consultant should pick an adviser that can (1) recognize qualifying engineering work embedded in project delivery, (2) document it to the standard the federal courts now apply, and (3) review client contracts for the funded research exclusion of IRC §41(d)(4)(H), which has defeated or sharply limited recent claims by a structural engineering firm and an architectural firm.

First, the Tax Court's June 16, 2026 memorandum opinion in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, applied the funded research rules to a major architectural practice and limited its credits to research costs exceeding client payments. Second, the IRS has made Section G (Business Component Information) of Form 6765 mandatory for most filers for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, which raises the documentation bar for every construction claim prepared from 2027 onward. In addition, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) restored current expensing of domestic research costs under new IRC §174A and reinstated the §280C(c) coordination rule, which changes the net value of the credit that consultants' estimators report.

Claims about the comparative performance of specialists versus general CPA firms (ROI ranges, detection rates, audit outcomes) come from promotional sources and should be treated as marketing assertions rather than evidence.
The Legal Baseline: What Any Consultant Must Apply
Qualified research under IRC §41(d)

The statute does not use that label, but the elements it describes are contained in IRC §41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a), and the label is the common shorthand used by practitioners, the IRS in examination materials, and the courts (the IRS conceded in Smith that the architectural work at issue satisfied "the four-part test"). Elements:

items: Permitted purpose (the section 174 and business component tests). The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component, and must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality (IRC §41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and §41(d)(3)). Research related to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors is not a permitted purpose (§41(d)(3)(B)). The expenditures must also be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures; for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, the cross-reference now runs to domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC §174A as well as §174.

Technological uncertainty. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3), uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component.

Technological in nature. The process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (IRC §41(d)(1)(B)(i); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(4)).

Process of experimentation. A process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset; the regulation names modeling, simulation, and a systematic trial and error methodology as examples (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5)). Substantially all of the activities (80 percent or more, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) must constitute elements of a process of experimentation, and the test is applied separately to each business component (IRC §41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6)). If the test is not met at the level of the whole product, the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2) applies it to successively narrower subcomponents, which is why the way a consultant defines business components matters so much in construction.

body.text: It is a reasonable practitioner test, and it echoes the regulation's focus on whether information available to the taxpayer establishes the method or design, but it is not the regulation's wording and should not be presented as a statutory element.
Qualified research expenses (QREs)

cells: Wages paid to an employee for qualified services, meaning engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research
Amounts paid for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research; land, depreciable property and general administrative services are excluded
Amounts paid to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research

65 percent of amounts paid to a person other than an employee for qualified research (75 percent for qualified research consortia; 100 percent for certain small-business, university and federal laboratory energy research)

body.text: Whether any individual's wages qualify depends on the time actually spent performing, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research, not on the title. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c), "direct supervision" means immediate first-line supervision, so the wages of senior executives or general project executives qualify only for the portion of time that meets that definition or that is spent directly performing research.
How the credit is computed

The statute sets the ASC at 14 percent of the amount by which current-year QREs exceed 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (IRC §41(c)(4)(A)). Correction: if the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, the ASC is 6 percent of current-year QREs (IRC §41(c)(4)(B)); the fallback applies whenever any one of the three years lacks QREs, not only when all three years are empty. The regular credit is 20 percent of QREs above a base amount computed from a fixed-base percentage and the average of the four preceding years' gross receipts, with a minimum base amount of 50 percent of current-year QREs (IRC §41(a)(1), §41(c)(1)–(3)).
Hypothetical example 1 (steady spending). A contractor has $1,000,000 of QREs in each of the three prior years and in the current year.

items: ASC: 14% × $500,000 = $70,000, which is 7% of current-year QREs.

body.text: Hypothetical example 2 (first claim or a gap year). The same contractor had no QREs in at least one of the three prior years: 6% × $1,000,000 = $60,000.

Hypothetical example 3 (net benefit after §280C(c)). For tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act amended IRC §280C(c) so that a taxpayer claiming the full credit must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditures (deducted under §174A or charged to capital account) by the amount of the credit, unless it makes an irrevocable reduced-credit election under §280C(c)(2) on a timely filed original return. The reduced credit equals the full credit minus the product of the credit and the maximum corporate rate (21 percent). Using example 1, a corporation electing the reduced credit would claim $70,000 × (1 − 0.21) = $55,300, or about 5.5 percent of current-year QREs, while keeping its full deduction.

Analysis: the 6 to 10 percent range is a fair rough guide to the gross ASC for firms with stable or modestly rising QREs, but it is an approximation, not a statutory rate. The estimator's other assumptions also need care: it applies 65 percent to all "subcontractor costs," while §41(b)(3) applies only to amounts paid for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf, not to subcontracted routine building work, and contract research is creditable only if the taxpayer bears the economic risk of failure and retains substantial rights (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)); its 75 percent payroll assumption is the tool's own input, not a rule.

Small construction firms should also know two related statutory features that a competent consultant will raise. A qualified small business (gross receipts under $5 million and no gross receipts more than five years before) may elect to apply up to $500,000 of the credit against the employer portion of payroll taxes for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 (IRC §41(h); §3111(f)). And eligible small businesses that meet the IRC §448(c) gross receipts test (about $31 million for 2025) could elect under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 to apply §174A, and the matching §280C(c) rules, retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021; the window for those amended-return elections closed on July 6, 2026 for most taxpayers.
Qualifying Construction Activities a Consultant Should Recognize
They are illustrations; each still has to pass the four statutory tests above at the level of a defined business component, and none qualifies merely because it appears on a consultant's list.

cells: Development of stadiums, dams, bridges and tunnels; improving a building's ability to withstand seismic events or extreme weather
Technical improvements to heat, light and power efficiency (CLA); functional, energy-efficient designs (KBKG)
Design and development of unique temporary systems such as shoring, formwork, falsework, power and dewatering systems
Moss Adams (2019); the original URL now redirects to a Baker Tilly page that does not repeat the list
Temporary works structure supporting an existing external wall, roof and basement on a heritage-listed project
The example is from Rift Research's UK page and concerns HMRC's UK regime, not IRC §41; it may illustrate the type of engineering uncertainty involved but is not US authority
Green building and sustainable design (CLA); LEED certification work (KBKG); modular and off-site methods and build sequencing (StrikeTax)

body.text: StrikeTax's page also lists what does not qualify: routine construction methods without experimentation or technical uncertainty, standard execution or scheduling, and off-the-shelf systems used without innovation. Those vendor statements are consistent with the statutory exclusions for research after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement, duplication, surveys and routine data collection, and routine quality control testing (IRC §41(d)(4)(A)–(D) and (G)). Analysis: a consultant's value lies in drawing that line accurately at the business-component level, which is precisely what the case law below tests. Note also that the regulations treat a building or structure itself as potentially a business component only to the extent the taxpayer's activities meet all four tests with respect to it; in practice, defensible construction claims usually identify specific systems, assemblies, connections, temporary works or processes rather than whole buildings.
Why Documentation and Scoping Decide Claims
Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (7th Cir. 2023)

Identification: Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), No. 21-3145, decided March 7, 2023, affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15. The taxpayer, parent of Corn Island Shipyard, Inc., claimed the credit for eleven first-in-class vessels; a tanker barge and a dry dock were treated as representative. The Seventh Circuit held that the taxpayer had not shown that substantially all (at least 80 percent) of its research activities were elements of a process of experimentation, and it rejected the taxpayer's argument that the novelty of most of each vessel was enough to meet the test. Because the taxpayer claimed whole vessels on an all-or-nothing basis rather than identifying subcomponents, the courts were unable to apply the shrinking-back rule.

Correction of emphasis: the Seventh Circuit rejected part of the Tax Court's reasoning while affirming the result. Most significantly, it rejected the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of pilot-model production wages from the numerator of the "substantially all" fraction, holding that pilot-model production activities can be elements of a process of experimentation, and it agreed with the taxpayer that direct support and supervision activities belong in both the numerator and the denominator. The court then held that the taxpayer failed the test under either assumption. Analysis for construction: the decision is favorable to claimants that build and test one-off temporary works or prototypes, but only if they can show, with records, how those activities were used to resolve specific uncertainties.
What strong documentation looks like

Source Advisors calls documentation the most challenging part of the R&D credit and recommends advisers that offer a structured data-gathering method and templates for contemporaneous records. Cherry Bekaert likewise recommends project- or task-level time tracking and defining R&D projects as specific systems or structural solutions rather than whole buildings.

Form 6765, Section G. The IRS redesigned Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, to include Section G, Business Component Information, which asks for each business component's description, the type of component, the information sought to be discovered, and the wages, supplies and contract research expenses allocated to it. In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS made Section G optional for all filers for tax year 2025 and announced that it will be mandatory for tax year 2026 and later, with optional reporting only for qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit and for taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less. The final instructions confirm that Section G applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Analysis: for construction and A&E firms, Section G converts the project-by-project scoping that the courts demanded in Little Sandy Coal into a filing requirement, so a consultant's ability to define business components and allocate costs to them is now a compliance capability, not merely an audit-defense one.

Separately, since 2022 the IRS has required research credit refund claims on amended returns to identify each business component, the research activities performed, the individuals who performed them, and the information each sought to discover, and it has extended the transition period in which taxpayers may perfect deficient claims. Construction firms considering a look-back study for open years should ask any candidate consultant how it meets those claim-for-refund requirements.
The Funded Research Exclusion and Contract Review
The rule

IRC §41(d)(4)(H) excludes from qualified research "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)." Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(1), amounts payable under an agreement that are contingent on the success of the research are considered paid for the product or result of the research, so the research is not treated as funded. If the performer retains no substantial rights in the research, it is treated as fully funded and the performer cannot claim it (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(2)). If the performer retains substantial rights and is not paid contingent on success, its research is funded to the extent of the payments it receives, and only expenses exceeding those payments can qualify (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d)(3)). The regulations under §1.41-2(e) apply the mirror-image rules to the customer side, which matters for owners and general contractors that pay engineers or specialty subcontractors to perform research for them.
Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner

The Tax Court (Judge Holmes) sustained the IRS on summary judgment in an order dated November 19, 2020 (Docket No. 7805-16), and the Eighth Circuit affirmed on May 6, 2024: Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 23-1523, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024). The appellate court reviewed the contracts de novo.
Facts from the opinion and commentary:

items: MBJ is a Minnesota structural engineering firm that prepares construction documents of the structural design for building projects; the tax years at issue ended September 30, 2010, 2011 and 2013. The Tax Adviser's and Bloomberg Tax's summaries put the denied credits at approximately $190,000.

The court found that none of MBJ's contracts expressly or by clear implication made payment contingent on the success of its research. Contract terms requiring professional skill and care did not mandate success, and MBJ cited no provision requiring refunds if it missed specific benchmarks. Commentators note the court compared MBJ's contracts to those in Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), which lacked rejection language or limits on payment to accepted work.

On fixed-price contracts, the court acknowledged the Tax Court's earlier statement in Populous Holdings that fixed-price contracts have generally been considered unfunded, but followed the Fifth Circuit's analysis in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), under which fixed-price status is relevant but not decisive. MBJ's inspection, acceptance and quality assurance provisions did not change the result.

body.text: It is The Tax Adviser's (September 30, 2025) characterization of the Geosyntec and Grigsby line of cases on which the Eighth Circuit relied, so it is paraphrased here rather than quoted as the holding. Later decisions, including Smith, read Meyer, Borgman & Johnson as requiring that success be measurable against specific, detailed criteria in the contract before payment can be treated as contingent on it.
Smith v. Commissioner (2026)

In Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026; Docket Nos. 13382-17 et al.), the Tax Court applied the funded research rules to Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP, an Illinois architectural partnership, for its 2008 through 2010 tax years. The IRS conceded that the work satisfied the four-part test, so the case turned on the funded research exclusion and on the reasonableness of partner compensation under §174(e). Of the six sample projects, two failed outright because the contracts transferred copyright in the work product to the client and restricted the firm's use of project information, so the firm retained no substantial rights. In the other four, the firm retained substantial rights, but milestone and phase-based progress payments meant it bore no economic risk of failure; the court treated that research as partially funded, so only QREs exceeding client payments could qualify, and it did not itself compute partial credits. The court also rejected the taxpayers' Loper Bright challenge to the validity of Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d), and it found the partners' compensation reasonable under the independent investor test.

Analysis: commentators disagree on emphasis (the firm's counsel described the decision as a taxpayer win because the credit was not eliminated on four projects, while other practitioners described the result as a largely denied claim), but the practical lesson for consultant selection is the same.
Fee Structures, Contractual Protection and Disclosure

items: Treas. Reg. §1.6011-4(b)(4) defines a transaction with contractual protection as one in which the taxpayer has the right to a full or partial refund of fees if all or part of the intended tax consequences are not sustained, or in which fees are contingent on the taxpayer's realization of tax benefits from the transaction.

Rev. Proc. 2007-20 exempts contingent-fee arrangements tied to certain credits, such as the low-income housing credit under §42 and the work opportunity credit under §51. The §41 research credit is not on the list, as CohnReznick (February 27, 2025) also notes, so a §41 engagement priced as a percentage of the credit can be a reportable transaction.

A taxpayer required to disclose must attach Form 8886, Reportable Transaction Disclosure Statement, to its return for each year of participation and send a copy to the IRS Office of Tax Shelter Analysis on first filing (Treas. Reg. §1.6011-4(d) and (e)).

body.text: That is the full statutory range across all reportable transactions, but the $200,000 maximum ($100,000 for a natural person) applies only to listed transactions. A transaction with contractual protection is a non-listed reportable transaction, for which the penalty is 75 percent of the decrease in tax shown on the return as a result of the transaction, subject to a minimum of $10,000 ($5,000 for a natural person) and a maximum of $50,000 ($10,000 for a natural person) (IRC §6707A(b); Treas. Reg. §301.6707A-1). The penalty is in addition to any other penalty, and the IRS Commissioner may rescind it only for non-listed transactions under §6707A(d).

Alternate Tax Solutions says it works on a fixed-fee basis and that many providers charge a share of savings, sometimes 25 to 35 percent. Source Advisors advises avoiding firms with high contingency fees or undisclosed pricing.

Fixed fees avoid the contingent-fee trigger, but CohnReznick lists audit guarantees and fee refunds among arrangements that can also raise contractual-protection questions. Firms should read the terms of any audit-protection offer, including a specialist's, with that in mind; an offer of free audit defense that is not conditioned on the tax result is different from a promise to refund fees if the credit is disallowed.
Selection criteria supported by the sources

Source Advisors lists six factors for choosing a specialist: industry-specific experience; technical and tax expertise (teams with engineers, attorneys and CPAs); a proven methodology with documentation support; audit support; transparent fees; and collaboration with the client's CPA. Analysis, in light of the law: a construction firm should also ask any candidate consultant

items: how it reviews client contracts for risk-of-loss and rights-retention terms under §41(d)(4)(H) after Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith, and whether it tracks research costs against client billings project by project;
how it defines business components to meet the 80 percent test and the shrinking-back rule after Little Sandy Coal, and how it will populate Form 6765, Section G for tax years beginning after 2025;
how it treats subcontractor payments under §41(b)(3) and the economic-risk and substantial-rights requirements of Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e);
whether its estimate is stated before or after the §280C(c) adjustment, and whether it has evaluated the reduced-credit election;
exactly what its audit support covers, whether any element is conditioned on the tax result, and whether its fee or guarantee terms could create contractual protection requiring Form 8886.

body.text: Claims About General Accounting Firms

items: ROI of 200% to 2,000% and recoveries of $100K to $1M+ annually. These figures appear in an Asnani CPA article about startup tax credits, with no stated methodology; they are not specific to construction.
General CPAs avoid credits they don't fully understand. Asnani CPA states this as opinion.
Generalists overlook qualifying activities. Source Advisors says a credible specialist can identify activities generalists may overlook. This is a vendor view, not data.

Louisiana contractor missed $62,034. NestWorth's case study describes an unnamed Louisiana contractor that believed the credit was for tech startups and, after review, identified $62,034 of credits for 2021 operations. Clarification: the contractor's own CPA raised the credit; the case is unnamed promotional material and cannot be independently verified.

body.text: Analysis: nothing in the statute, regulations or case law distinguishes between specialist consultants and general accounting firms; the credit belongs to the taxpayer, and the taxpayer bears the burden of substantiation whoever prepares the claim. The relevant distinction is capability: whether the adviser, of whatever type, can perform the technical interviews, contract review, business-component scoping and Section G reporting that the law now requires.
Conclusion

Little Sandy Coal (2023) penalized whole-project claiming without activity-level records; Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (2024) denied a structural engineering firm's credits because its contracts did not make payment contingent on research success; and Smith (2026) confirmed that copyright transfers and milestone billing can eliminate or limit an architectural firm's credit. Mandatory Section G reporting for tax years beginning after 2025 and the reinstated §280C(c) coordination rule add a compliance and valuation layer that every consultant must now handle.
Analysis: those are the criteria on which to judge any consultant, specialist or generalist.
